sections.h2: How can sellers contact the Guernsey County Recorder?
sections.html:
Per the county recorder page, the office opens at 8 a.m. and closes at 4 p.m. on weekdays. Call 740-432-9275, or send a fax to 740-439-6267. Cambridge is the county seat and largest city, and the auditor works from the Administration Building at 627 Wheeling Avenue.

Ohio recorders hold the ownership record for land and each lien against it. A seller whose own deed was never recorded should expect the buyer's title company to pause the sale until that gap is closed.

sections.h2: Does Guernsey County take electronic deeds?
sections.html:
Yes. Four submitting vendors can send eRecordings to the recorder, a route used mostly by lenders, banks, attorneys and title companies. Only document types that the office takes by regular mail qualify, and each vendor sets its own price.

A second route, described on the auditor's page, is e-filing through Kofile Technologies. Transmission is open every hour of every day, but staff process files only between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. on weekdays, so a late upload waits a business day. Plats and military discharges (DD-214) cannot go this way. When a deed or conveyance form is rejected, processing restarts once the corrected version arrives.

sections.h2: What happens at the Guernsey County Auditor before recording?
sections.html:
Real estate staff there move the deed onto the tax records and then pass it to the recorder. Its suite is 301 at 627 Wheeling Avenue, and the phone is (740) 432-9243, option 1 for real estate. Forms for sellers and closing agents include:

  • DTE 100, the real estate conveyance form, and DTE 100 EX for exempt transfers
  • DTE 101, the statement of conveyance of homestead property
  • DTE 102, the statement of conveyance of CAUV property
  • A routing sheet and a timeline for deed transfers
  • Transfer and Conveyance Standards effective October 1, 2022

A conveyance fee calculator sits under tools on the auditor's site. State fees come from R.C. 319.54 ($1.00 per thousand) and R.C. 322.02 (a county transfer tax of up to 30 cents per hundred dollars), so rely on the calculator or a phone call for the Guernsey County total.

sections.h2: What does the conveyance statement ask in Guernsey County?
sections.html:
R.C. 319.202 governs the form. A buyer or the buyer's representative files it ahead of the auditor's endorsement. It declares the property's value, meaning the whole price with any mortgage or vendor's lien included, and willfully falsifying that figure is prohibited.

The same statute adds questions on tax reductions and farm status:

  • Either an affirmation that the seller was asked about a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the current or prior year's taxes, or a sworn statement giving the reduction and its estimated amount.
  • Either an affirmation about current agricultural use valuation (CAUV) status, or a sworn statement noting a possible recoupment charge.
  • The reason for any exemption, written on the form when no fee is due.

After endorsement the auditor retains the original, sends a copy to the tax commissioner and hands one to the buyer. Residential rental property gets an added notice telling the buyer to register with the auditor.

sections.h2: What fees apply at the Guernsey County Recorder?
sections.html:
Charges track R.C. 317.32. Combined, the Ohio Recorders' Association table reads $34.00 for the opening two pages, $8.00 per page after that and $4.00 per marginal notation, with up to $5.00 per document for preservation. Half of every fee funds basic recording and the other half the state's Housing Trust Fund.

The table also lists a $10.00 plus $10.00 standardization fee for a document that misses the formatting rules. Ask the recorder at 740-432-9275 whether Guernsey County adds the surcharge, because that choice rests with each county.

sections.h2: Who can notarize a deed signed in Guernsey County?
sections.html:
After the grantor signs, someone from the list in R.C. 5301.01 has to witness the acknowledgment. That list takes in notaries, mayors, the auditor, the engineer, and judges or court clerks. Banks, title companies and law offices usually keep a notary on staff.

R.C. 5301.25 sends each deed to the county of the land and labels an unrecorded one fraudulent as against a later buyer acting in good faith. A deed made after a survey must carry the surveyor's name.

sections.h2: How does a homestead reduction affect a Guernsey County sale?
sections.html:
The auditor's information page explains the homestead rules that sit behind the statement questions above. A homeowner qualifies by owning and occupying the home as a principal residence on January 1 of the year of application, and by meeting one of three tests: age 65 by December 31 of the filing year, total and permanent disability, or being the surviving spouse of a past recipient who was at least 59. Owners with more than one home count as living where they are registered to vote and where their federal income tax form places them.

Ohio returned to income testing in 2013, but anyone who received the credit for tax year 2013 keeps it without an income limit. Disabled veterans with a qualifying federal rating receive a reduction equal to the tax on $50,000 of true value, compared with $25,000 for the standard credit, and the spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty receives the same $50,000 level with no income limit.

sections.html:

The auditor's delinquent tax notice cites R.C. 5721.03 and warns that listed parcels will be certified for foreclosure or a tax certificate sale unless every delinquent tax, assessment, interest and penalty is paid within a year. If the seller's parcel is on the list, pay it at or before closing.

sections.h2: What does Census data show for Guernsey County owners?
sections.html:
Guernsey County lies in the Appalachian foothills, organized in 1810, with about 522 square miles of land, and the auditor counts 40,170 parcels. Census estimates give 38,379 residents in 2025, about level with 2020, and 22.1 percent are 65 or older.

Owners hold 72.1 percent of homes, with a $157,700 median in the 2020 to 2024 survey, while renters pay a $864 median gross rent. Median household income is $58,478, and 41 building permits were issued in 2025. The auditor's forms list includes a Mineral Deeds section, so ask the buyer's title company to search for any recorded mineral deed or lease on the parcel.

sections.h2: How large are Guernsey County households and neighborhoods?
sections.html:
There are 16,318 households averaging 2.31 people, and 19,116 housing units as of 2025. Monthly owner costs have a median of $1,237 with a mortgage and $505 without one. Broadband reaches 86.4 percent of households.

Density is 73.6 people per square mile, and the average commute takes 22.9 minutes. Four townships passed to Noble County in 1851, and the county borders Tuscarawas, Coshocton, Harrison, Noble, Muskingum and Belmont counties. Buffalo, Kimbolton and Salesville are census-designated places outside Cambridge, and deeds for land there are recorded in the same Cambridge office.

faqs.q: When is the Guernsey County Recorder open?
faqs.a: Weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. Call 740-432-9275, and note that electronic filings get processed only until 3 p.m.

faqs.q: Can a deed be eRecorded in Guernsey County?
faqs.a: Yes, through one of four submitting vendors or through Kofile e-filing. Plats and military discharges are excluded, and a title company usually handles the upload.

faqs.q: Does the deed go to the auditor or the recorder first?
faqs.a: The auditor, who transfers it on the tax records with a conveyance form and then forwards it to the recorder. The auditor posts a timeline for deed transfers.

faqs.q: What is the basic recording charge in Guernsey County?
faqs.a: The Ohio Recorders' Association table shows $34.00 for two pages plus $8.00 for each more page, and up to $5.00 as a preservation surcharge. Check with the recorder about any county surcharge.

faqs.q: What is the risk of leaving a deed unrecorded?
faqs.a: R.C. 5301.25 treats it as fraudulent against a later buyer who acted in good faith without notice. Record it as soon as the auditor has transferred it.
